item.name: Ridge House 01
item.description: The westernmost house on the ridge, set lowest on the slope and organised around a long south-west living terrace.

item.name: Ridge House 02
item.description: A west-facing ridge house with a double-height stair hall that carries evening light down into the bedroom level.

item.name: Ridge House 03
item.description: The most compact of the ridge houses, planned around a single continuous living space that runs the depth of the plan.

item.name: Ridge House 04
item.description: The last of the ridge houses, with the deepest terrace and the only external stair down to the plateau path.

item.name: Terrace House 05
item.description: The first of the five terrace houses: a narrow, deep plan stepping down the slope in three half-levels.

item.name: Terrace House 06
item.description: A mid-row terrace house with the same stepped section and a longer, quieter garden at the rear.

item.name: Terrace House 07
item.description: The largest terrace house, with a fourth half-level under the roof drawn as a studio rather than a bedroom.

item.name: Terrace House 08
item.description: The smallest house in the development and the entry point to the ridge, planned for two people who occasionally host four.

item.name: Terrace House 09
item.description: The end-of-row terrace house, turned to catch the south-west light and given a second parking bay.

item.name: Courtyard House 10
item.description: A single-storey courtyard house on the plateau, where the ridge flattens and the wind decides the plan.

item.name: Courtyard House 11
item.description: The middle courtyard house, with a second, smaller service court that separates the guest rooms from the family wing.

item.name: Courtyard House 12
item.description: The highest and largest house, holding the end of the plateau with a five-bedroom plan around a single deep court.

itemListElement.name: Why twelve houses and not forty

@graph.headline: Why twelve houses and not forty
@graph.description: The ridge could carry three times the density under the local plan. The arithmetic of why it does not is the whole argument of the project.

mainEntity.name: What happens after I send this form?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your request is recorded immediately with a reference code beginning AST- and passed to the sales team. A person answers within 24 hours, Monday to Saturday.

mainEntity.name: How long does a visit take?

acceptedAnswer.text: About ninety minutes. Visits leave from the sales office at Rua da Pedreira 12, Oeiras, and cross the ridge on foot, so sturdy shoes are genuinely necessary.
Not yet. Two houses are under construction and can be walked through in shell form. Everything else is seen as drawings and on the ground itself.

mainEntity.name: Will I be added to a mailing list?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Requesting a visit consents to us answering that request only. Marketing contact would need a separate opt-in, which this form does not ask for.

@graph.name: The ridge itself
@graph.description: A 1.4 km limestone escarpment at 148–178 m, carrying the twelve plots, a retained vineyard and an orchard.

@graph.name: Pedra Alta village
@graph.description: The nearest settlement: a square, a weekly market, a pharmacy, two restaurants, a bakery and the primary school.

@graph.name: Oeiras and the coast
@graph.description: The nearest town centre and the Atlantic: supermarkets, international schools, the marina, and the coast road west.

@graph.name: Central Lisbon
@graph.description: Twenty-two kilometres east: the reason the ridge is commutable and the reason it is quiet.
